readerTitle: Hiring your first engineer when you can't read code
caseNote: 가상 사례 (회계·기장 서비스 회사, 철물 도매 유통업체) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 첫 엔지니어 채용은 기술 목록이 아니라 '혼자 해내야 할 결과'를 정하고, 그 결과와 닮은 일을 직접 시켜 보는 것으로 판단한다. 코드를 몰라도 평가할 수 있다.
misconception: 코드를 모르면 엔지니어를 평가할 수 없으니, 긴 기술 목록과 유명 회사 경력을 기준으로 뽑아야 한다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 PPL-03-01 (역할 정의), PPL-03-03 (실무 능력 테스트)을 적용한 레슨
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 외부 연구나 통계는 인용하지 않았습니다. 고객 200곳, 직원 12명, 창고 3곳, 반나절 과제 등은 모두 가상 수치입니다. 게시 전 연구 수치를 추가하려면 1차 출처를 붙이세요.
유료 과제의 적정 시간·보상 수준은 나라와 업계마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 특정 금액이나 법적 기준을 쓰지 않고 '짧게, 보상하고, 모두 같은 과제'라는 원칙만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Hiring your first engineer when you can't read code
body: Dana runs a 12-person bookkeeping firm. Her 200 clients still email spreadsheets and blurry receipt photos every month.
She wants an engineer to build a client portal. Her first job ad asks for React, Python, cloud, mobile, AI and "rockstar energy." She has no idea how she'd judge any of it.

image.label: A job ad covered in tech buzzwords on a cluttered office desk
image.brief: 작은 회계 사무실 책상. 노트북 화면에 기술 용어가 빽빽한 채용 공고 초안, 옆에 영수증 사진과 스프레드시트 출력물이 쌓여 있음. 대표가 머리를 긁는 모습. 실제 로고나 상표 없이.

cards.title: What should the job post lead with?
body: Dana will get one shot at a first post. What goes at the top?

options.text: A full list of technologies, so strong engineers see we're serious
options.feedback: A long tool list attracts people who match keywords, not people who can do this job. It also scares off the generalists who fit best.

options.text: What they must deliver: a secure portal for 200 clients, built and run mostly alone
options.feedback: This is **defining the role**: start from outcomes. Candidates can judge if they've done something like it, and Dana gets a yardstick she can actually use.

options.text: A job description copied from a well-known tech company
options.feedback: It reads professionally, but that role sits inside a big team. Dana's engineer will have no team at all.

cards.title: What this role actually involves.
body: Seen this way, Dana needs a builder who has shipped something alone and kept it running, not a specialist from a large team.

breakdown.label: Engineer
breakdown.detail: No senior colleague to check the work

breakdown.label: Upkeep
breakdown.detail: Whoever builds it keeps it running

cards.title: Outcomes change who you look for.
body: **Defining the role** means writing down what success looks like after six or twelve months, before you write a single requirement.

Dana's version: "Clients upload documents through a secure portal. Staff stop chasing email. The system runs without drama." From that, the must-haves are short: has built and maintained a small product, explains choices simply, picks boring, reliable tools.

cards.title: Dana can't read code. How does she test candidates?
body: Three candidates look good on paper. She needs to see who can really do the work.

options.text: Use hard coding puzzles found online
options.feedback: Puzzles test speed under pressure, not building a portal. And Dana still can't judge the answers.

options.text: A short, paid task: turn a messy sample spreadsheet into a simple upload page, then explain it to Dana
options.feedback: This is **testing real skills**: a small slice of the actual job. Dana judges the explanation; a freelance engineer she hires for a few hours judges the code.

options.text: Pick the one who worked at the most famous company
options.feedback: A big name suggests ability, but not the ability to work alone. It tells you about their old team as much as about them.

cards.title: The task looks like the job.
body: One candidate built a polished page but couldn't say why. Another built something plainer, flagged a privacy risk in the sample data, and explained it in two minutes.
The outside reviewer confirmed the second candidate's code was clean and easy to maintain. Dana could see the most important skill herself: clear thinking for non-engineers.

image.label: An engineer explaining a simple upload screen to a business owner
image.brief: 회의 테이블에서 지원자가 노트북의 단순한 업로드 화면을 대표에게 설명하는 장면. 화면 한쪽에 작은 경고 표시(개인정보 주의). 옆에 외부 검토자가 코드 화면을 보고 고개를 끄덕임. 실제 로고 없이.

cards.title: A good test can still go wrong.
body: Work tasks cost candidates time. Keep them to a few hours, pay for them, and never use them to get free work you plan to ship.
Give every candidate the same task and the same scoring notes, or you're comparing apples to oranges.
And a task is one signal. A strong result doesn't replace checking how someone works over months.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware wholesaler.
body: Marco's family business supplies hardware stores from three warehouses. Staff phone each other to check stock before confirming orders. He wants a first engineer to connect orders and stock counts.

options.text: Define the outcome as "orders and stock match daily across all three warehouses," then test with real but anonymized order data and a talk with the warehouse lead
options.feedback: Both ideas at work: **defining the role** sets the bar, and **testing real skills** shows who can handle messy data and floor staff.

options.text: Hire whoever is most impressive over coffee
options.feedback: Fast and friendly, but it tests charm, not the ability to untangle three warehouses of data.

options.text: Define the outcome clearly, but skip the test because a trusted friend vouches for one candidate
options.feedback: A clear role is half the job. Without a task, though, you're betting on someone else's view of a different kind of work.

cards.title: Define the result, then watch them do a piece of it.
body: You used two ideas: **defining the role** (outcomes before tools) and **testing real skills** (a small, paid slice of the real job). Together they let anyone hire well outside their own expertise.
**Try it today:** for your next hire, write one sentence on what must be true in six months. Then sketch a two-hour task that looks like that work.
